column1: # Operating system functions. One row per function, per task it belongs to. Tab-separated; see finder.py for the rules.

column7: summary
Returns command-line argument n, the program's name for 0, or all of them if omitted.
Runs a command through the system shell, waits, and returns its exit code or -1.
Runs a program by its path with arguments, waits, and returns its exit code or -1.
Runs a program without arguments, waits, and returns its exit code or -1.
Hands control to another program and ends this one; returns -1 if it cannot start.
Returns the value of an environment variable, or an empty string if it is not set.
Sets an environment variable from "NAME=value" text; returns 0 on success.
Returns the folder that holds the running program.
Returns the current folder.
Changes the current folder; returns 0 on success or -1 on failure.
Creates one folder, whose parent must already exist; returns 0 on success.
Removes an empty folder; returns 0 on success or -1 on failure.
Returns the first name matching a pattern, then the next one on each later call.
Copies a file, overwriting the destination; returns 0 on success.
Renames or moves a file or folder; returns 0 on success.
Deletes a file; returns 0 on success or an error code.
Returns non-zero if the file exists, or 0 if it does not.
Returns the size of a named file in bytes.
Returns when a file was last modified, as a date serial.
Returns an open file number's mode, system handle or encoding.
Writes buffered output for one or all open files to the system, or on to disk.
Cuts or extends an open file so that it ends at the current position.
Closes all open files and ends the program, with an optional exit code.
Returns the amount of free physical memory, in bytes.
Returns non-zero if standard output, or input if asked, is redirected to a file.
Returns every command-line argument as Unicode text, the program first, empty ones kept.
Holds a program and its arguments, passed exactly as given with no shell in between.
Runs a Command with this program's console, waits, and returns its exit status.
Runs a Command, waits, and returns its exit status and all it wrote to stdout and stderr.
Runs a command line through cmd.exe or /bin/sh, waits, and returns its exit status.
Adds one argument and returns the Command, so calls chain.
Adds every string in an Array as an argument.
Sets the folder the program starts in.
Sets one environment variable for the program only.
Removes one environment variable for the program only.
Starts the program with an empty environment, which Env calls then add to.
Connects the program's stdin, stdout or stderr to this console, to nothing, or to a pipe.
Sends the program's stderr wherever its stdout goes.
Starts the program in its own process group, so Windows can send it Ctrl-Break.
Starts a console program on Windows without opening a console window.
Returns the command line quoted as the system will see it, for logs.
Names where a stream goes: STDIO_INHERIT, STDIO_NULL or STDIO_PIPE.
Holds one running program; destroying it leaves the program running.
Starts the program a Command describes, or returns why it could not.
Returns the running program's process id.
Returns the pipe to the program's stdin, stdout or stderr when the Command asked for one.
Closes the program's stdin, waits for it to end, and returns its exit status.
Waits up to a number of milliseconds; returns the exit status, or none if still running.
Returns the exit status if the program has ended, or none if it is still running.
Ends the program at once.
Asks the program to stop; on Windows it ends it at once, as Kill does.
Holds one end of a pipe to a program, read and written like any other stream.
Holds how a program ended: its exit code and, on Linux and macOS, the ending signal.
Returns the program's exit code, or -1 on Linux and macOS when a signal ended it.
Returns true if the exit code is 0.
Returns the signal that ended the program on Linux and macOS, or 0.
Holds a finished program's exit status and the bytes it wrote to stdout and stderr.
Returns what the program wrote as UTF-8 text, with U+FFFD for any bad bytes.
Returns an environment variable's value, or an empty Optional when it is not set.
Sets an environment variable for this program and the programs it starts.
Removes an environment variable; removing one that is not set succeeds.
Returns every environment variable as a map of names to values, sorted by name.
Replaces $NAME and ${NAME} in text, and %NAME% on Windows, with the variables' values.
Turns Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Break and requests to stop into a flag, instead of ending the program.
Returns true once an interrupt has arrived; never waits.
Waits for an interrupt and returns true, or false if the time runs out first.
Returns which kind of interrupt arrived, such as INT_CTRL_C, or INT_NONE.
Returns how many interrupts have arrived since the last reset.
Clears the interrupt flag and the count.
Gives Ctrl-C and the other signals back to their default handling.
Names the kinds of interrupt: Ctrl-C, Ctrl-Break, terminate and hang-up.
Returns a Context cancelled by the first interrupt, so goroutines stop on Ctrl-C.
Holds "windows", "linux" or "macos", the system the program was built for.
Holds "x86_64", the processor the program was built for.
Returns the Windows version number, or the kernel release on Linux and macOS.
Returns the computer's network name, or an error.
Returns the name of the user running the program, or an error.
Returns this program's process id.
Returns this program's process id, the same number as ProcessId.
Returns how many processors this program may run on, which can be fewer than exist.
Returns the memory page size in bytes.
Returns the computer's physical memory in bytes, or 0 if it cannot be found.
Returns true if stdin, stdout or stderr is an interactive terminal.
Ends the program with an exit code, running module destructors and flushing files.
Ends the program at once, with no cleanup at all.
Holds why a std/os call failed: a code, the system's error number and a message.
Returns the message text for a std/os error code, such as "invalid argument".
Holds why a program could not be started or waited for: a code, a number, a message.
Returns the message text for a std/process error code, such as "program not found".
